note: Phase 30 of the brief: a bad educational system sees concepts everywhere.
These cases are written BEFORE the concepts they constrain. Each names a surface pattern
that naive recognition would latch onto, and the condition under which the concept does NOT
apply. A concept listed here may not reach stage 'ready' until it carries an engine-tested
counterexample covering its case — tools/run_tests.py enforces that.
fen: null means the position has not been constructed yet; that is itself a tracked gap.

cases.surface_pattern: A knight sits on a central advanced square such as d5.
cases.why_not: An outpost requires that no enemy pawn can challenge the square. If ...c6 or ...e6 is available, the knight is merely visiting.
cases.resolution: Resolved by two independent checks. This base's own Layer 3 detector reports that d5 is NOT a hole for White and returns an empty outpost list, because Black still has the e7 pawn and can play ...e6 - so the system does not make the false positive in the first place. The engine agrees there is nothing to claim: Black stands at +0.74. Note that the question is definitional rather than evaluative, so the detector, not the engine, is the instrument that settles it.

cases.surface_pattern: A rook reaches the opponent's seventh rank.
cases.why_not: The rank matters when it attacks pawns, confines the king, or supports an invasion. A rook on an empty seventh with the enemy king already safe achieves nothing and can be driven away with tempo.
cases.resolution: Resolved. A black rook sits on the seventh with an empty rank to work on and an enemy king that already has luft, and the position is level at -0.04. The two conditions the concept record names as what makes a seventh-rank rook strong are both absent, and the rook is correspondingly worth nothing.

cases.surface_pattern: Two friendly pawns share a file.
cases.why_not: Doubling can open a file for a rook, add central control, and shield a king. Weakness depends on whether they can be attacked and whether they are immobile.
cases.resolution: Resolved twice over. The Ruy Lopez Exchange position, where Black has just accepted doubled c-pawns, evaluates at exactly 0.00. And the cost of inflicting them is measurable from the position one move earlier: 4.Bxc6 is +0.08 where the quiet retreat 4.Ba4 is +0.42, so doubling the opponent's pawns was worth minus 0.34 to the player who did it. The bishop pair and the half-open file pay for the structural damage.

cases.surface_pattern: A bishop sits behind its own pawn chain.
cases.why_not: A bishop hemmed in by pawns on its own colour may still be the key defender of a colour complex, or may become excellent after one pawn break. Mobility, role and prospects matter, not geometry alone.
cases.resolution: Resolved by building the detector the concept needed. lib/features.js now measures both halves of the distinction the record insists on: how many of a side's own pawns share the bishop's colour (structural) and how many squares the bishop actually sees (functional). The matcher requires BOTH before reporting a bad bishop, so Suba's active bad bishop - structurally bad, sees eleven squares - is not reported. The position was found by searching 1576 real positions for the shape rather than constructed to fit. A first version also reported undeveloped bishops on their home squares, which was caught by the existing false-positive regression suite.

cases.surface_pattern: A king has lost its pawn cover or sits in the centre.
cases.why_not: With the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often simply an active king. Exposure matters in proportion to the attacking force that remains.
cases.resolution: Resolved by proof. Both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter whatever - the feature detector reports pawnShield 0 for each - and the tablebase says the position is a draw. King safety is phase-dependent: once the pieces that could punish exposure are gone, the exposed king is not merely safe but is where it should be.

cases.surface_pattern: The queen leaves its starting square in the first few moves.
cases.why_not: The guideline exists because the queen can be harassed with tempo. Where no such harassment exists — the Scandinavian after ...Qa5, or 2.Qh5 lines that have concrete point — the objection does not apply.
cases.resolution: Tested and only partly as expected, which is why it is recorded as partially resolved. The Scandinavian is a sound opening whose queen comes out on move two, so an early queen move must not be reported as an error - that much holds. But it does NOT escape the tempo cost: White is +0.76 here against +0.30 after 1...e5. The correct statement of the false positive is therefore narrower than first written - the pattern must not be flagged as a mistake, but neither should the base claim such openings pay nothing.

cases.surface_pattern: The same piece moves twice inside the first ten moves.
cases.why_not: Concrete gain overrides the guideline: capturing, escaping a threat, or reaching a decisively better square all justify it. This is the brief's own example of principle yielding to tactics.
cases.resolution: Resolved decisively. In the Ruy Lopez after 3...a6, moving the same bishop a SECOND time with 4.Ba4 is the best move at +0.42, against +0.08 for 4.Bxc6 and +0.04 for 4.Bc4. The repeated piece move is not merely acceptable but worth roughly a third of a pawn more than any alternative, in one of the most frequently played positions in chess.

cases.surface_pattern: A pawn has no friendly pawn on either adjacent file.
cases.why_not: An IQP grants central space, two open files and outposts on the squares beside it. It is a dynamic asset in the middlegame and a static liability in the endgame; which dominates depends on how much material remains.
cases.resolution: Resolved. In a standard isolated-queen's-pawn position the side WITH the isolani stands slightly better (+0.14 for White). The isolated pawn buys space, an active bishop and the squares in front of it, and at this stage that is worth marginally more than the structural liability. An isolated pawn must therefore never be reported as a weakness on sight.

cases.surface_pattern: A pawn has no enemy pawn ahead of it on its own or adjacent files.
cases.why_not: A passed pawn that is permanently blockaded by a minor piece is a target rather than an asset, and it can cost tempi to defend.
cases.resolution: PROVEN draw. White has a passed h-pawn, an extra bishop, and the more active king, and cannot win. The pawn is passed and worthless because it is a rook pawn whose promotion square the bishop does not cover. Paired in this base with the identical position with the bishop on the other colour, which is a proven win in 9 - same material, same passed pawn, opposite result.

cases.surface_pattern: A file has no pawns of either colour.
cases.why_not: A file is worth occupying only if it offers entry squares. A file whose seventh and eighth ranks are covered gives a rook nothing but a stare.
cases.resolution: Resolved. A symmetric position with the d-file open and a rook of each colour on it evaluates at +0.02 - dead level, with the best line simply trading the rooks. An open file is not an advantage in itself; it is an advantage only when one side can use it and the other cannot.

cases.surface_pattern: One side is ahead on the standard 1/3/3/5/9 count.
cases.why_not: Piece values are a heuristic for counting, not an evaluation. Compensation in activity, king safety or structure regularly outweighs a pawn or the exchange.
cases.resolution: PROVEN draw with an extra BISHOP AND an extra PAWN. A material count says roughly +4; the truth is a dead draw, because the h-pawn promotes on a square the bishop cannot control and the defending king simply sits in the corner. This is the cleanest available demonstration that counting material is not evaluating a position.

cases.surface_pattern: A move gives check.
cases.why_not: Checks are forcing, not good. A check that drives the king somewhere better, or loses a tempo the attacker needed, is a mistake. This is the commonest beginner misconception in the base.
cases.resolution: PROVEN by the Syzygy tablebase, and controlled in the strongest possible way: this one position contains TWO checks with opposite results. Ra7+ holds the draw; Rg8+ LOSES. The surface pattern 'a check is available' therefore carries no information at all about whether checking is right - in this position it is simultaneously the drawing move and the losing move, depending only on which check. Rh8 and Rf8 also lose, so three of the seventeen legal moves throw away a proven draw.

cases.surface_pattern: A capture or trade is available and the player is materially or positionally ahead.
cases.why_not: Simplification is a method for reducing counterplay, not a rule. Which position you simplify INTO is the whole question, and a trade can convert a won position into a proven draw.
cases.resolution: PROVEN by tablebase, every legal move checked. Rb8 is mate in one. The only capture, Rxh7+, is also a check and is a proven draw, since after Kxh7 only the two kings remain. The one move that simplifies is the one move that throws the game away.

cases.surface_pattern: Few pieces remain and a king has left its back rank, so a material-based phase test calls it an endgame.
cases.why_not: King activation is a claim about a phase in which mating attacks have become unlikely. A material-based phase test can call a position with both queens on an endgame, and centralising into that is an invitation rather than a plan. Shereshevsky separately documents rook endings where centralisation is not merely untimely but wrong.
cases.resolution: Partially resolved and recorded as such. The concept now carries an explicit trap forbidding the recommendation while the opponent has a queen, and the matcher's guard (phase must be endgame AND pawns must be on) is documented as NOT covering this case. A full resolution would mean the matcher itself checking for enemy queens, which is a change to Layer 4 rather than to the record, and is listed as open.

cases.surface_pattern: Each side has exactly one bishop and they run on opposite colours.
cases.why_not: Drawish only when they are nearly the last pieces on the board. With other pieces present the same feature favours the ATTACKER, because each bishop guards a complex the other cannot contest.
cases.resolution: Registered from a near-miss position found by searching 1576 real positions for the surface pattern WITHOUT the concept's condition, then scored by the engine. Level-2 validation: the position was scored, not designed. It confirms the feature is present in real play and, where the score is near level, that the feature is not drowned out. It is not a controlled pair and proves nothing about the concept on its own.

cases.surface_pattern: A king sits on its back rank with no empty escape square.
cases.why_not: The pattern is only dangerous if a rook or queen can reach the back rank. With the heavy pieces gone it costs nothing.
cases.resolution: Registered from a near-miss position found by searching 1576 real positions for the surface pattern WITHOUT the concept's condition, then scored by the engine. Level at -0.24. A king with no luft is only in danger from a piece that can reach the back rank, and with the heavy pieces gone the missing escape square costs nothing. Recorded because the back-rank pattern is one of the easiest features to detect and one of the easiest to over-report.

cases.surface_pattern: One side has both bishops and the other does not.
cases.why_not: The pair's value comes from covering both colours in an OPEN position. In a closed one with no open file, it is worth little and a knight may be the better piece.
cases.resolution: Registered from a near-miss position found by searching 1576 real positions for the surface pattern WITHOUT the concept's condition, then scored by the engine. Level-2 validation: the position was scored, not designed. It confirms the feature is present in real play and, where the score is near level, that the feature is not drowned out. It is not a controlled pair and proves nothing about the concept on its own.

cases.surface_pattern: The fixed geometric facts of the board — colour-boundedness, the knight's colour change, and the fact that a king's diagonal path costs no more than a straight one.
cases.why_not: The rule of the square must be applied with the side to move in hand. This base holds a tablebase-proven pair where the identical position is a draw or a mate in 23 depending only on whose turn it is.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: The conventional numeric values of the pieces, and the properties those numbers compress away.
cases.why_not: Counting material is not evaluating a position. This base holds a PROVEN DRAW a bishop and a pawn up.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: Kings facing each other with one square between them on a rank or file. The side NOT to move has the opposition.
cases.why_not: Kings facing each other is trivially detectable and means nothing outside endgames where king penetration decides.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: A rook pawn whose promotion square is the opposite colour to the bishop's. Bishop and wrong rook pawn cannot win against a king that reaches the corner — the extra material is worth nothing.
cases.why_not: Being in front of the pawn is NOT enough, unlike king-and-pawn endings. The defending king must reach the corner or the square beside it — Mednis gives a position where the same setup wins with White to move and draws with Black to move.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: A file with none of your own pawns on it but one of the opponent's — so your rook looks straight at a pawn that cannot run away sideways.
cases.why_not: A semi-open file is a fact about pawns; whether it produces pressure depends on whether the target is fixed and whether you can attack it more times than it can be defended.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. Quiet and close to balanced at 0.91, which is the combination this base most needs and least often finds: nothing forcing is available and the evaluation is not swamping the feature, so the position is usable as an instance of the concept. What is NOT claimed is that the concept explains the engine's choice of move.

cases.surface_pattern: The drawing method against a rook pawn on the sixth: the defending rook attacks the pawn from the SIDE along the rank, never from behind, with the defending king tucked on g7 or h7.
cases.why_not: It is specialist theory for the ROOK PAWN on the sixth. Applying the side-attack idea to a central pawn does not work.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: What a player receives in return for material given up.
cases.why_not: Being down material with active pieces is not the same as having compensation. The Halloween Gambit position has active pieces and measures 1.75 pawns worse.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. Activity without compensation. 4.Nxe5 gives a knight for a pawn and produces a genuinely mobile centre and gain of time against the black knights, yet evaluates at -1.67 against +0.08 for the best move. Direct evidence that visible activity is not the same thing as adequate compensation, which is the trap this concept most needs guarding against.

cases.surface_pattern: An opening in which material, usually a pawn, is deliberately offered for non-material compensation.
cases.why_not: A pawn offered in the opening is not automatically a gambit with compensation. The Halloween Gambit is measured here at 1.75 pawns worse than the best move.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. A gambit with no adequate compensation, measured. 4.d4 +0.08, 4.Bb5 +0.03, 4.Nxe5 -1.67 - a loss of 1.75 against the best move. The investment of a knight for one pawn is not repaid by the resulting centre. Recorded as a counterexample deliberately: it is what stops this base from treating 'a gambit was played' as evidence that compensation exists.

cases.surface_pattern: Sacrificing one or two pawns to force through a passer the enemy king cannot catch.
cases.why_not: A pawn sacrifice that creates a passer is not a breakthrough unless the passer actually cannot be stopped. The rule of the square decides this and is cheap to check.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. The claim is confirmed exactly and the margin is enormous. The analogous breakthrough 1.b5 evaluates -5.86 and is NOT best; the quiet 1.a5 at -0.46 is. So the same pattern, with the pawns one rank further back, swings from +64.85 (winning by force) to -5.86 (losing) — a difference of over 70 pawns produced by one rank of space, with material and structure held identical. This is the cleanest confirmation in the base

cases.surface_pattern: A square in one's own camp that can no longer be controlled by a pawn, and that the opponent can use.
cases.why_not: Every pawn move creates squares no pawn can guard, so the raw feature fires everywhere. Usability is what makes it reportable.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. Quiet and close to balanced at 0.79, which is the combination this base most needs and least often finds: nothing forcing is available and the evaluation is not swamping the feature, so the position is usable as an instance of the concept. What is NOT claimed is that the concept explains the engine's choice of move.

cases.surface_pattern: A single weakness can usually be defended, because the defender can concentrate every piece on it. Creating a second target far from the first stretches the defence past what it can cover, and somethi
cases.why_not: Two weaknesses that the defending king stands between are not two weaknesses in the operative sense. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending, moving the kings to d3/d6 costs the attacker over half the advantage.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: Bxh7+ against a castled king, followed by Ng5+ and Qh5 — a bishop given to strip the h-pawn and drag the king out.
cases.why_not: The pattern is extremely recognisable, which is exactly why it is played in positions where it does not work. Vukovic's conditions are necessary, NOT sufficient.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. Bxh7+ collapses from BEST at +6.71 to LAST at +3.77 — a swing of 2.94 pawns, and from 1.41 ahead of the field to 1.59 behind it, on one defender of g5. The concept's central precondition is confirmed. HONEST QUALIFICATION: +3.77 still means White is much better, because White is much better in this constructed position for unrelated reasons — the sacrifice throws away most of an advantage rather than losing outright.
